Why can hot water sometimes freeze faster than cold water? In 1963, Erasto Mpemba noticed this while making ice cream, sparking a scientific mystery that still puzzles physicists. The Mpemba effect now appears in materials, magnets and quantum systems, revealing surprising connections between energy, equilibriu
items.why_watch: The Mpemba effect — hot water sometimes freezing faster than cold — sounds like a simple pub trivia fact, but Be Smart digs into why physicists still can't fully agree on the mechanism after 60 years of investigation. The video walks through competing explanations (evaporation, dissolved gases, convection currents) without oversimplifying, so you leave with a genuinely richer understanding of the phenomenon rather than a tidy but false answer.

items.title: The Lives of the TWELVE CAESARS By C. Suetonius Tranquillus - Sergius Galba
items.description:
The Twelve Caesars, is a set of twelve biographies of Julius Caesar and the first 11 emperors of the Roman Empire written by Gaius Suetonius Tranquillus. The group are: Julius Caesar, Augustus, Tiberius, Caligula, Claudius, Nero, Galba, Otho, Vitellius, Vespasian, Titus, Domitian.

The work, written in AD 121 during the reign of the emperor Hadrian, was the most popular work of Suetonius, at that time Hadrian's personal secretary, and is the largest among his surviving writings. It was dedicated
items.why_watch: Galba's brief, chaotic reign (68–69 AD) is one of the stranger chapters in Roman history — a severe, elderly general who seized power after Nero only to alienate nearly everyone within months. Suetonius's gossipy, detail-rich style makes this a surprisingly readable primary source, and an audiobook format means you can absorb it without sitting down at a screen.

discovery_articles.title: Kloster Eberbach in Eltville am Rhein, Germany
discovery_articles.snippet: Perched on a sun-drenched slope in Eltville am Rhein, Kloster Eberbach stands as a masterpiece of Cistercian architecture, founded in 1136 by twelve monks seeking isolation and spiritual rigor. The abbey is famous for its vast, column-free Romanesque grain barn and its historic wine cellars, which have been producing Rheingau Rieslings for nearly nine centuries, making it a pivotal site in the history of European viticulture. Its atmospheric stone corridors and vaulted halls became globally recognized as the setting for the 1986 film adaptation of Umberto Eco’s The Name of the Rose , starring Sean Connery, which utilized the abbey to depict the grim, intellectual world of a 14th-century Italian monastery.
